site.title: Arcade Patches
site.tagline: Translations, restorations and arranged soundtracks for classic arcade games.
intro: A lot of great arcade games never made it out of Japan, and plenty of others had their best material added later, on the home ports. Re-recorded soundtracks, cutscenes the arcade version never had, characters that turned up years afterward. The patches here put that work back onto the arcade hardware it belongs on.
Each one runs against your own copy of the game, on a real board, on a MiSTer, or in MAME. No game data is hosted here, and nothing goes out until it has been tested on the real thing.

sections.title: Audio Arrangements
sections.description: When Capcom brought its arcade games home on CD, it re-recorded the music. These put those soundtracks back under the arcade games on MiSTer, while every punch, voice and jingle still comes from the board.

sections.title: Enhanced Versions
sections.description: Arcade games with the best of their later versions built in: characters, modes, cutscenes and more from the home ports, running as real arcade games. The originals stay intact underneath.

sections.title: Restorations
sections.description: Some games lost things on the way out of Japan: quotes, endings, even characters, or the ability to run outside Japan at all. Others never left Japan, or never reached the arcade in their final form. A restoration brings the Japanese game back, in English where it needs it, and leaves the rest of the game as it was.

projects.title: CPS+
projects.subtitle: Arranged CD-era soundtracks for CPS-1 & CPS-2 arcade games on MiSTer
projects.hardware: MiSTer FPGA (CPS-1.0, CPS-1.5 and CPS-2 cores)
projects.summary: When Capcom brought its arcade games home on CD, it sent the music back to the studio and re-recorded it. Those versions never made it back to the arcade. CPS+ puts them there. Pick a game on your MiSTer and the arranged soundtrack is just playing, while every punch, voice and jingle still comes from the arcade board itself.
projects.featured_stats: 27 audio packs · 80 MRAs · 3 cores · every pack built from sources you own
description: From Final Fight CD onward, Capcom kept sending its arcade soundtracks back to the studio. Every CD-based home port got a full re-recording of the music, the 'arrange' versions, produced by the original composers' teams. For thirty years those recordings stayed locked to the home versions. CPS+ puts them where they always belonged, under the arcade games themselves.

On a MiSTer, the real CPS-1 or CPS-2 hardware logic runs the game while the CD-era soundtrack plays the music, started, looped and faded by the game itself, exactly the way Capcom's own console releases timed it. Hit sounds, voices and the announcer stay pure arcade. It sounds like the arcade board grew a CD drive.

Version 1.3 brings the arranged soundtracks to two new Super Turbo projects, Grand Master Challenge and Super Street Fighter II EX: The Ultimate Championship, with either the Anniversary Edition arrangement or the HD Remix soundtrack. It also moves the Final Fight EX and Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold MRAs onto those projects' latest sets.
how_it_works: Nothing in the game is modified. CPS-1 and CPS-2 games post sound commands to their audio hardware, and the CPS+ core watches for them. When one matches the loaded pack, it streams that arranged track and holds the command back from the sound chip. Everything else plays as it always did: hit sounds, voices, the announcer, and the jingles a pack deliberately leaves alone.
The trigger tables were reverse-engineered from Capcom's own console releases and checked against the arcade programs, down to the loop points and fades.

A pack carries the arranged tracks and the table that says which sound command starts each one. The MRA points at the pack, and MiSTer loads it into memory alongside the ROM. A stock MiSTer runs all of this as it comes.
A given disc always produces the same pack, and the builder checks yours against a published hash.
download_notes: The download is tools: the MRAs, the three CPS+ cores with their GPL-3.0 source, and the pack builder. It makes the packs on your machine from discs, disks and albums you own, naming anything it skips for want of a disc. It also assembles out/mister/ for you, holding the cores, your packs, and only the MRAs those packs can load, so nothing on the card fails to start.

Five MRA groups pair CPS+ audio with sets that are not stock: the Alpha 2 Gold MRAs load the SFA2 Gold reconstructed sets, the Grand Master Challenge and Super Street Fighter II EX MRAs load those projects' HBMAME sets, ‘Final Fight EX (Arrange)’ loads the Final Fight EX set, and ‘Final Fight 30th Anniversary CPS2 Edition (Arrange)’ loads the CPS2 conversion of Final Fight that the Arcade Offset project distributes. Build the first four with their own kits first (links below).
quickstart: Edit builder/discs.toml and point it at the disc rips you own (each entry is optional), or pass them on the command line with --disc mtwins_pce_disc=/discs/chiki.7z. make_packs.py --list shows every pack and the disc it wants.

Run python3 builder/make_packs.py (Python 3.11+, numpy, ffmpeg). It builds out/mister/, laid out like your SD card. The three X68000 packs also need git, cmake and a C/C++ compiler, and take up to an hour each to render. The Strider pack needs MAME and your PlayStation BIOS set, and takes about five minutes to record.
Copy the contents of out/mister/ to your MiSTer SD card, merging with what's there. Arcade ROM zips go where they always do.
tech_spec: Community packs are a first-class goal, so the format is documented and the tools ship in the kit. build_pack.py init <game> starts a project; you supply the tracks and say which sound command triggers each one; build_pack.py build produces the pack, which you can listen through, check, and point an MRA at.
Any QSound CPS-2 title is a potential target, and CPS-1 and CPS-1.5 games work too. PACK_FORMAT.md in the kit covers the trigger contract, the pack layout, and how to author one.

projects.coverage_intro: Every soundtrack is built from one disc, one set of disks, or one album you own. Where a disc came out in several regions, the ones listed below all produce the same pack.

faq.q: What do I need installed to build the packs?
a: Python 3.11 or newer, numpy, and ffmpeg on your PATH. On a Mac: brew install python ffmpeg, then pip3 install numpy. On Linux, use your package manager. 7-Zip is only needed if your rips are .7z archives. The three X68000 packs additionally need git, cmake and a C/C++ compiler (see the X68000 question below). The Strider pack needs MAME as well (see the Strider question below).
Nothing is installed on the MiSTer itself. The kit is plain files copied to the SD card, and a stock MiSTer runs them as-is.

faq.q: What disc rip formats does the builder accept?
a: A .cue sheet with its .bin files beside it, a .mds/.mdf pair, or a .zip/.7z archive containing exactly one cue sheet. For the PlayStation 2 sources, point it at the .iso (or a zip containing it). The two CD-audio sources (the Final Fight OST and the Area 88 soundtrack) are folders of .flac or .wav files instead of a disc image. The X68000 games are a zip of their .dim or .xdf floppy images. The two album sources are the downloads themselves: Capcom's Double Impact zip, as downloaded or unpacked, and the OC ReMix folder holding the FLACs. The Strider PlayStation disc can be .chd, or .cue with its bins.
CHD rips need converting back first with chdman extractcd, since the builder doesn't read CHD directly.

faq.q: A pack failed hash verification. What now?
a: It almost always means the disc isn't one of the supported releases listed above, or the rip is damaged. Check which release you have, re-rip if in doubt, and run make_packs.py again. A nonstandard ffmpeg build can also encode slightly differently; the stock Homebrew or distro ffmpeg matches the published hashes.
The builder won't stage a pack that fails, so a bad rip can't reach your SD card. There's a --no-verify flag if you want one anyway.

faq.q: What do the X68000 soundtracks need, and why are they different?
a: The X68000 ports of Ghouls'n Ghosts, Street Fighter II' Champion Edition and Super Street Fighter II shipped their music as MIDI, meant for a Roland SC-55 on the desk next to the computer. There is no recording to copy, so the kit renders one on your machine, the same way the published packs were made: your disk images, your SC-55 ROM set, and a cycle-accurate SC-55 emulator built from source at a pinned revision.

That means git, cmake and a C/C++ compiler (Xcode's command-line tools on a Mac, build-essential and cmake on Debian or Ubuntu), a one-time build of a few minutes, and then ten minutes to an hour of rendering per game. The result is hash-checked like every other pack. The kit's X68000.md walks through it.

The published packs were rendered and rebuilt byte-for-byte on a Mac. Whether the emulator's output is bit-identical on every CPU has not been proven; if it isn't on yours, the builder stops at the hash check rather than staging different audio.

faq.q: What does the Strider pack need, and why is it different?
a: The PlayStation port's Sound Remix music is sequenced and played by the game's own sound driver through the console's sound chip, so there is no recording on the disc to copy. The kit makes one: MAME boots your disc, walks into the game's sound test, plays the ten performances and records the console's output. The builder then cuts the reviewed performances from that recording and checks each against its published hash.

That means MAME installed (brew install mame on a Mac, your package manager on Linux, the official build on Windows), your Strider (USA) disc as .chd or .cue, and MAME's PlayStation ROM sets, psu.zip and psx_cd.zip, in a folder you point discs.toml at. The recording takes about five minutes. The kit's PSX.md walks through it.

The pack was verified with MAME 0.288 from Homebrew on a Mac and with the official Windows build. Those two record a few samples a tiny, inaudible step apart, so the kit accepts both and checks each against its own hashes. If your MAME build renders differently, the builder stops at the hash check rather than staging different audio.

faq.q: Will this touch my existing MiSTer setup?
a: No. The CPS+ cores have their own names and the MRAs live in their own folder, so your existing cores, MRAs and ROMs are untouched. To remove it, delete the _Arcade Patches folder, the three cores and games/CPS+.

faq.q: Is any of the music in the download?
a: No, the kit is tools only. Every pack is made on your machine from a disc you own.

faq.q: Do the packs work in MAME or on a real arcade board?
a: No. CPS+ is a MiSTer feature: the streaming player lives in the FPGA cores and the pack loads into the MiSTer's DDR memory. Everywhere else the games just play their stock music.
The companion projects do cover other targets: SFA2 Gold, Final Fight EX, Grand Master Challenge and Super Street Fighter II EX all ship HBMAME sets. See their pages, linked below.

faq.q: I built the 1.2 packs. Do I need to rebuild them for 1.3?
a: No. Every pack you built with 1.2 still works with 1.3. Three packs (the two Double Impact remixes and HD Remix) have new reference hashes, because they now build to the same bytes on every computer, but the difference is inaudible and the files are the same size. Copy the new MRAs to your card.
If you use the Gold, Final Fight EX or Grand Master Challenge MRAs, rebuild those sets with their projects' latest kits: the MRAs now expect the new sets.

faq.q: I built the 1.1 packs. Do I need to rebuild them for 1.2?
a: Six packs changed. The three Final Fight soundtrack packs (SNES, X68000 FM and X68000 MIDI) now start their opening where the arcade's own song starts, in both regions, and leave the phone ring to the board. The three Super Street Fighter II packs (Arrange, Turbo Arrange and X68000 MIDI) now let the QSound logo jingle play from the arcade board. Ten SSF2-family MRAs also changed, carrying each region's factory EEPROM defaults.

Drop the 1.2 kit over your old one, add the new sources to discs.toml, and run make_packs.py again. Every pack it builds is checked against the published hashes, so the six changed ones come out corrected and the rest come out identical, and out/mister/ picks up the new MRAs. The other 17 packs and the three cores are unchanged, hash for hash.

items: A second player joining at the character select no longer kills the music. The board borrows the music channels for the “Here comes a new challenger” stinger and hands them back; the packs read that as a new song, so the arranged track stopped and nothing restarted it. Affects the Street Fighter II family: Super Street Fighter II, Turbo, Hyper, and the X68000 and HD Remix soundtracks. The board's own stinger is heard under the arranged music, and HD Remix's arranged stinger is no longer in the pack.

Fixes the pack builder: building any of the three album-sourced packs (Final Fight and Magic Sword Double Impact, Super Turbo HD Remix) stopped with a KeyError at the last step. The packs themselves are unchanged — each still builds to the same bytes as before.
The kit's README now states the version it was built as.
Super Street Fighter II Turbo: Grand Master Challenge, with the Anniversary Edition arrangement or the HD Remix soundtrack, loading the restoration's HBMAME set.
Super Street Fighter II EX: The Ultimate Championship, USA and Japan, with the same two soundtracks. The bonus stages keep the board's own music.
Final Fight (Arrange + CD Cutscenes) is now Final Fight EX (Arrange), and loads the Final Fight EX rc2 sets.
The Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold MRAs load the rc3 sets.

Builds on Windows: paths pasted straight into discs.toml work, the X68000 tools build with MinGW or Visual Studio, .zip and .7z sources both work, and the Strider pack records and verifies with MAME's official Windows build.

Every pack now builds to the same bytes on any computer. The Double Impact and HD Remix packs used to come out slightly different on Intel and AMD PCs; their reference hashes change by an inaudible amount, and a pack you already built keeps working.

If a pack doesn't verify, make_packs.py now tells you which disc track differs and why (a different rip, a read offset, a missing track), and fixes rips that are only shifted. --check-inputs checks your discs without building.
Six new MRAs (80 in all). The three cores are unchanged.

Final Fight and Magic Sword with the remixed soundtracks from Final Fight: Double Impact (Simon Viklund; Melssen and Thunberg), built from Capcom's free 2010 soundtrack download. Final Fight's is one pack for both regions.
Super Street Fighter II and Super Street Fighter II Turbo with the OC ReMix soundtrack from Super Street Fighter II Turbo HD Remix, built from OC ReMix's official FLAC release.
Strider with the Sound Remix performances from its PlayStation port, recorded from the game's own sound test with MAME on your machine.

Fixes: the three Final Fight soundtrack packs (SNES, X68000 FM and X68000 MIDI) now start their opening where the arcade's own song starts, in both regions, and leave the phone to the board; the Super Street Fighter II packs let the QSound logo jingle play from the arcade board; the SSF2-family MRAs carry each region's factory EEPROM defaults.
Twelve new MRAs (74 in all) and four new packs (27 in all). Six existing packs changed (see the FAQ); the other 17 packs, their MRAs and the three cores are unchanged.

X68000 MIDI soundtracks for Street Fighter II' Champion Edition, Super Street Fighter II and Ghouls'n Ghosts / Daimakaimura, rendered on your machine from your own X68000 disk images and SC-55 ROMs.
Final Fight 30th Anniversary CPS2 Edition with the Sega CD arrangement, from the same US Final Fight CD as the CPS-1 pack.
Ten new MRAs (62 in all) and five new packs (23 in all). The eighteen 1.0 packs, their MRAs and the three cores are unchanged, so nothing needs rebuilding.

patches.title: Night Warriors 2
patches.subtitle: English translation
patches.summary: Vampire Hunter 2 never left Japan. This translates all of it, under the Western name it should have had: Western character names, all 225 post-fight quotes, every boss exchange, and every ending.
description: Vampire Hunter 2 is a Japan-only follow-up to the game the West knew as Night Warriors: Darkstalkers' Revenge. It never came out in English. This patch translates the entire game and gives it the name it should have had, Night Warriors 2.

Where Capcom's own English exists, in the Western Night Warriors and Vampire Savior and the PlayStation Darkstalkers 3, the patch uses it, as long as it says what the Japanese says, so it reads like the official localization. The rest gets a fresh translation, written to read naturally while staying true to the original: the victory quotes, the boss exchanges, and every ending.
The Night Warriors 2 title screen isn't a fan mock-up. An unused Western title was already sitting inside the original game, and the patch finishes it and switches it on.

USA region presentation
Western character names on character select, route map, and fight HUD: Zabel → L.Raptor, Gallon → J.Talbain, Lei-Lei → Hsien-Ko, Phobos → Huitzil, Aulbath → Rikuo
All 225 post-fight quotes in English, using Capcom's own wording where it matches the Japanese
All boss dialogs and every ending translated
Route stage names and the staff roll in English
Capcom's misspelled "L.Rapter" name art corrected to L.Raptor
Oboro Bishamon's win plays his own victory music, as intended

patches.title: Street Fighter Alpha 3 Upper
patches.subtitle: NAOMI GD-ROM multi-region patch
patches.summary: Zero 3 Upper shipped locked to Japanese cabinets. One byte in the disc header says so. Change it, re-encrypt it, and the same disc boots on a USA or Export NAOMI.
description: Street Fighter Zero 3 Upper is an enhanced version of Street Fighter Alpha 3 that only came to arcades in Japan, on Sega's NAOMI hardware. Because it's flagged as a Japanese release, a US or Export machine rejects the disc on sight with "THIS GAME IS NOT ACCEPTABLE BY MAIN BOARD."

This patch flips that region flag so the very same disc boots on Japanese, US, and Export systems. Nothing about the game itself changes. On a US or Export machine it now comes up with its Western Street Fighter Alpha 3 branding instead of the Japanese Street Fighter Zero 3, exactly as an overseas release would have.
It is the smallest change possible. Only the region flag is touched, and the game, its language and its settings are left just as Capcom shipped them.
changes: NAOMI header region mask: Japan → Japan + USA + Export (one byte in the game header, eight encrypted bytes on disc)
Nothing else. This is a region unlock only, and it does not translate or otherwise modify the game

screenshots.caption: The same patched disc on two BIOS regions. The game's own region-dependent title art shows Street Fighter Zero 3 on a Japanese board and Street Fighter Alpha 3 on a USA board. Note the U.S. copyright line under the American title.
A USA-region NAOMI BIOS: the original Japanese GD-ROM is refused; the patched image is accepted and loads.

notes: Applying the patch requires chdman (bundled with every MAME release) and about 2.5 GB of temporary disk space.
MAME reports a checksum warning for the patched CHD. This is expected; the game boots and plays normally.
For optical drive emulators on real hardware, the patched CHD can be unpacked to GDI with chdman extractcd.
You still need the unchanged sfz3ugd.zip (security PIC) alongside the CHD.

patches.title: Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold
patches.subtitle: Zero 2 Dash, rebuilt for CPS-2 hardware
patches.game: Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold / Zero 2 Dash (2006 PlayStation 2 anthology revision)
patches.summary: Capcom's 2006 PlayStation 2 anthology carried the final revision of Alpha 2 Gold, the console edition of Alpha 2 that brought Cammy into the roster. It was never released on arcade hardware. This rebuilds it as a real CPS-2 game, in four regional builds, for emulators, MiSTer, and real hardware.
description: Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold, known as Zero 2 Dash in Japan, was the console revision of Alpha 2 that added Cammy as a playable fighter, first on PlayStation and Saturn and in final form in Capcom's 2006 PlayStation 2 anthology. It was never released on arcade hardware. This project rebuilds the anthology's edition as a real CPS-2 game.

It is a faithful reconstruction, not a remix. It starts from the original arcade Zero 2 Alpha program and restores the anthology's changes piece by piece: Cammy, her graphics, the audio, and the endings, each one checked against the PlayStation 2 original. Four regional builds are provided, shown below. The English builds also carry the full Japanese script, newly translated: every story and ending page, Evil Ryu's own ending, and all 452 win quotes.
This is a release candidate.
changes: Cammy restored as a playable fighter, with her graphics, palettes, voice, sound effects, win poses, and ending
Cammy's own stage music: her X-Men vs. Street Fighter theme, played on Alpha 2's own sound hardware
Shin Akuma selectable: press Start five times on Akuma at player select
The revised title, presentation, and staff-credit screens for each region
In the English builds, the full Japanese script in English: every story and ending page, Evil Ryu's own ending, and all 452 win quotes, plus red blood and Birdie's missing victory pose
Four regional builds: USA (Alpha 2 Gold), Europe (Alpha 2 Dash), Japan (Zero 2 Dash), and an English Asia (Zero 2 Dash)
4 MB builds for real hardware and stock MAME, plus 8 MB builds carrying Cammy's full audio for HBMAME and MiSTer

screenshots.caption: Cammy joins the roster on the character-select screen.
Cammy in action, landing a jumping kick on Guy.
Shin Akuma is selectable too: press Start five times on Akuma.

requires: your own PlayStation 2 anthology disc image: Street Fighter Alpha Anthology, or Street Fighter Zero — Fighter's Generation for the Japan set
your own arcade Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha romset: sfz2al, plus sfz2alj for the Japan set
reconstruction.kit_command:
python3 apply.py --iso "Street Fighter Alpha Anthology.iso" \
                 --romset sfz2al.zip --region us --out-dir out

notes: The 8 MB builds hold more QSound audio than an original CPS-2 board supports, so they run only on HBMAME and MiSTer, not real hardware.

This is a fan reconstruction, unaffiliated with Capcom. The sets are built from discs and roms you already own, and the kit ships no code or data from the anthology or the arcade game, with one exception: Cammy's stage music uses about 4 KB of her theme's score from X-Men vs. Street Fighter (Capcom, 1996), which the kit carries.

items: Cammy's stage music is restored. You can hear it in a two-player match.
Portraits before a fight and in the story scenes no longer pick up the wrong colors.
In the English builds, the last lines of every ending now display in full, and ending text sits clear of the screen edges.
The English builds (USA, Europe and Asia) now carry the whole Japanese script in English. Every story and ending page is back, in the Japanese order, including scenes the English version cut short.
Evil Ryu has his own ending again, with his narration and his scene with Akuma, instead of borrowing Ryu's.
All 452 win quotes from the Japanese game, in English, picked by opponent and remaining health the way the Japanese game does it, and centered on screen. Cammy keeps her four Gold quotes.
Story, ending and quote text is translated from the Japanese. Where Capcom's English said the same thing, it's kept.
Red blood on hits in the English builds, as in Japan.
Birdie's third victory pose is back; the English builds showed another pose in its place.
The Manual guard panel on the select screen now explains itself. It appears when the operator turns on Auto Guard.
Every set has new checksums, so rebuild them with the rc3 kit.
Fixed a sprite corruption that appeared during the attract sequence.
Polish improvements to the title screens across all four regions.
All four builds are rebuilt and set checksums have changed, so rebuild your sets with the rc2 kit.
First public release.

patches.title: Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha
patches.subtitle: English restoration · The Japanese script, all of it
patches.patch_intro: An unofficial fan restoration of Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha (Asia 960826): the Japanese game's full story, endings and win quotes, in English.
patches.summary: Zero 2 Alpha's English script was a cut-down one: shorter story scenes, a handful of random win quotes, and no ending of his own for Evil Ryu. This puts the whole Japanese script back, in English.
description: Street Fighter Zero 2 Alpha is the updated Alpha 2, and its Asian board plays in English. But that English script was a shortened one. Story scenes lost pages, Evil Ryu borrowed Ryu's ending, and each fighter picked from four random win quotes instead of the hundreds the Japanese game has.

The English Restoration is the Japanese script, in English. Every story and ending page is back, in the Japanese order. Evil Ryu has his own ending again, and his scene with Akuma. All 452 win quotes are here, picked by who you beat and how much health you had left, just like in Japan. Where Capcom's English said the same thing as the Japanese it's kept; everything else is newly translated.
A few smaller things come along: red blood on hits, as in Japan; Birdie's third victory pose, which the export board swapped out; and the Manual guard panel on the select screen now explains itself.

The fighting is untouched, and the ROM sizes and key stay stock, so it drops in over the Asian set in MAME, HBMAME, on MiSTer or on a real CPS-2 board. The same restoration is in the English builds of Street Fighter Alpha 2 Gold.
This is a release candidate. It has been checked in MAME, route by route; a MiSTer hardware pass is still to come.

patches.title: Final Fight EX
patches.subtitle: The Sega CD cutscenes, on the arcade board
patches.summary: The Sega CD version of Final Fight opened with a proper animated cutscene. Final Fight EX puts it back on the arcade game, running as native CPS-1 graphics, with a new EX title, for HBMAME and MiSTer.
description: The 1993 Sega CD port replaced the arcade's brief story block with a fully animated opening and a soundtrack with spoken dialogue. Final Fight EX reproduces that cutscene as native CPS-1 presentation on the arcade Final Fight, driven by a new 68K cutscene engine added to the game's program ROM, and gives it a new EX title screen. The stock game, its timing, and its gameplay are left intact.

The cutscene art needs far more room than a stock Final Fight board has, so the graphics region is grown from 2 MB to 6 MB. An original CPS-1 board and stock MAME cannot address that extra ROM, so this runs only on HBMAME and on MiSTer's jtcps1 core.

There are two regional builds, USA (ffightus01) and Japan (ffightjs01), each matched to its own disc. You supply the arcade Final Fight romset and your own Final Fight CD, and the build is put together on your machine.

This is the visual half. The cutscenes play over the arcade game's own music and effects. The Sega CD's soundtrack and spoken dialogue are a separate release, the CPS+ arrange packs, which ship their own MiSTer MRA combining the two. Install this on its own and you get the cutscenes with arcade audio.
changes: The Sega CD opening cutscene rebuilt as native CPS-1 graphics: the Metro City map, the Mad Gear line-up, Damnd's sketch and the knife, Haggar's phone call, and the Cody & Guy montage

patches.subtitle: English restoration · Japan's Super Turbo
patches.game: Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge (Japan 940311)
patches.patch_intro: An unofficial fan restoration of Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge (Japan 940311): the Japanese game, in English, under a US identity.
patches.summary: Japan's Super Turbo is the one the pros play, and it never came west. Now it does: the same game, with every quote, tip and ending in English.
description: Super Turbo came in two versions. Japan got Super Street Fighter II X, the one competitive players swear by. The rest of the world got a slightly different game: it plays differently, the continue screen is bare, most of the win quotes are gone, the endings are shorter, and Akuma's story is missing. Japan's version, of course, was in Japanese.

Grand Master Challenge is Japan's game in English. The fighting is untouched. Everything you read is new: all 136 win quotes, the strategy tips on the continue screen, the full endings, and Akuma's dialogue, translated fresh from the Japanese with Capcom's own English as the style guide.
It runs anywhere Super Turbo does: MAME, HBMAME, MiSTer, or a real CPS-2 board. The patch keeps the ROM's original sizes and key, so it drops in over the stock Japanese set.

items: The English was checked line by line against Capcom's own US script. Wherever Capcom's wording kept the Japanese meaning, it's now used: 54 lines across the win quotes, the endings and the Tournament Battle rules. Chun-Li's "Men are no challenge at all", for one, is now "You're no challenge at all". The Japanese story points stay, like Shoryuken instead of Sheng Long, and Cammy's spy story.
Every ending now plays out exactly as it does in Japan. Some scenes were being skipped under the US region, like Jane and Amy arriving to stop Guile.
Ending text looks like the US game's again: the fighters' lines in blue, everyone else in pink, and every caption centered in its box.
Akuma's reply to M. Bison is complete: "I am your shadow. Those possessed by the shadow must die. Your time is up!"
Dhalsim's teleport tip now explains that your input decides where he reappears.
Only sfxj.03d changes, so rebuild your set with the rc2 kit.

patches.patch_intro: An unofficial fan edition of Super Street Fighter II X: Grand Master Challenge (Japan 940311): Shin and Ten Akuma, the bonus stages, Tournament Battle and more, in a USA build and a Japanese build.
patches.summary: Japan's Super Turbo with the extras it never had together: Shin Akuma and Ten Akuma on the select screen, the bonus stages back, Tournament Battle, two more colors and Free Play. In English or Japanese.
description: Super Turbo is the version competitive players swear by, but it left things behind. The bonus stages from Super Street Fighter II were gone. Shin Akuma was a hidden boss you had to earn, and Ten Akuma only turned up years later at home. Tournament Battle, the eight-player linked-cabinet mode, stayed with the earlier Super Street Fighter II.

EX puts it together on the arcade game. Shin and Ten Akuma are playable from the start, picked from Ryu. The car, the falling barrels and the oil drums are back between fights. Link cabinets with the adapter and it runs Tournament Battle; without it, it plays as normal. Every fighter gets two more colors, the move names are the modern ones, and the new title reads The Ultimate Championship.
Nothing about the existing fighters changes: this is Japan's Super Turbo underneath. The USA build carries all of Grand Master Challenge's English text; the Japan build keeps the Japanese.
EX keeps the board's own ROM layout: the same files as the Japanese set, so it runs in MAME, HBMAME and on MiSTer, and on a real CPS-2 board.
This is a release candidate.

patches.patch_intro: An unofficial fan restoration of Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter (Japan 970707): the Japanese board's content, in English, in a USA build and a Japanese build.
patches.summary: The US board left things out: no Norimaro, generic endings for the secret fighters, and half the win quotes. This puts it all back, in English, and changes nothing else.
description: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter wasn't the same game everywhere. The Japanese board has Norimaro on the select screen with his own ending, real endings for Mech-Zangief, Shadow and Dark Sakura, and sixteen win quotes per fighter. The US board dropped Norimaro entirely, gave the secret fighters a generic ending, and cut the win quotes to eight.

The English Restoration is the Japanese game, in English. Norimaro is back, with his ending. The secret fighters get their own endings and art. All sixteen win quotes per fighter and all seventeen standard endings are translated fresh from the Japanese.

Nothing else changes. The title, the secret-character codes, the team rules and the bosses are exactly as they were, and the fighting is untouched. If you want more, like playable bosses, any team you like, extra colors and eight speeds, that's EX, which includes everything here.
There are two builds. The USA build is the English one. The Japan build keeps its Japanese text and gets the few fixes that apply to it. Both run in MAME, HBMAME and on MiSTer.
This is a release candidate. Both builds boot and have been checked in MAME; longer play testing and a MiSTer hardware pass are still to come.

patches.summary: The arcade game with everything it held back: Norimaro in the US game, Cyber-Akuma and Apocalypse on your side, extra colors and eight speeds. USA and Japan builds.
description: Marvel Super Heroes vs. Street Fighter kept a lot from you. Outside Japan there was no Norimaro. Nowhere could you play as Cyber-Akuma or Apocalypse, or put the same fighter on a team twice. The console ports later added extra colors and more speeds, but only at home.

EX gives the arcade game all of it. Norimaro is on the select screen in both builds, with his own ending. Hold Start on any fighter for two seconds and their hidden version appears, no codes needed, though the old codes still work. Any two fighters make a team. Cyber-Akuma and Apocalypse are playable too: hold Start on Akuma for one, on Norimaro for the other. Every fighter gets the Saturn version's two extra colors, on the HP and HK buttons, and the service menu goes from three speeds to eight.

The fighting itself is untouched: no changes to moves, damage, hitboxes or the computer. The USA build also gets a new translation, straight from the Japanese: sixteen win quotes per fighter instead of eight, and every ending retold. It comes in two builds, USA and Japan, both with Free Play, and runs in MAME, HBMAME and on MiSTer.
This is a release candidate. Everything builds and boots; longer play testing and a MiSTer hardware pass are still to come.

patches.patch_intro: An unofficial fan restoration of Vampire Savior: The Lord of Vampire (Japan 970519): the Japanese board's content, in English, in a USA build.
patches.summary: The export boards toned Vampire Savior down: less blood, recolored gore, dropped win quotes and endings cut short. This is the Japanese game, in English, with all of it back.
description: Vampire Savior wasn't the same game everywhere. The export boards recolored Jedah's blood purple and Forever Torment's green, cut a few gory touches entirely, and defaulted to sweat instead of blood. Their English script dropped fourteen win quotes and 47 ending pages. Even the damage values differ: in places the export boards hit a little harder.

The English Restoration is the Japanese board, in English. The blood is red again, everywhere it was in Japan. All 241 win quotes and every ending page are here, translated from the Japanese: where Capcom's English said the same thing it's kept, and everything else is newly translated, including the pages the export dropped. The fights run on Japan's damage values and Japan's computer difficulty.

Out of the box it's set up like a Japanese cabinet: blood on, Auto guard selectable at the select screen, one coin one credit. The operator menu and the Western character names stay as the US board has them, and Lord Raptor's name finally reads L.Raptor instead of L.Rapter.
It's a USA build that runs in MAME, HBMAME and on MiSTer. The Japanese board already has everything above, so there's no Japan build for now.
This is a release candidate.
